text: This is an illustrative case study, not a real reported incident. Meridian Finworks needed a custom role for its CI/CD service principal -- routine access to restart app services and scale VM scale sets during deployments, scoped to one production resource group. Under deadline pressure, the role got assigned at the subscription level instead.

The role definition itself had a problem: Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachineScaleSets/* is a wildcard at the resource-provider level, granting every action on every scale set, not just restart and scale. But AssignableScopes listing the whole subscription, and the actual assignment being made there, was the bigger issue -- scope and permissions are two separate dimensions, and both were too wide.

The result: a service principal meant only to touch one app resource group could reach VM scale sets, diagnostic settings, and authorization data across the entire subscription, including the data platform's own resources that had nothing to do with deployments.

Nobody caught this in a planned access review. It surfaced sideways, through a routine Defender for Cloud recommendation flagging a service principal with unusually broad write access. A security engineer ran az role assignment list against that identity and found one assignment, at subscription scope, for a custom role nobody currently on the team remembered writing.

This mattered even though the service principal had never actually used most of what it could reach -- the deployment pipeline only ever touched one resource group. That's exactly the danger: a future compromise of this identity, the kind of incident Lesson 30 just walked through, would have reached the whole subscription instead of being contained to the one resource group the pipeline actually needed.

The fix re-scoped the assignment down to that single resource group, replaced the wildcard action with the two specific actions the pipeline calls, and swapped the custom role entirely for two combined built-in roles. Meridian also added a standing review specifically for subscription-scope custom role assignments, since that one pattern was the actual root cause. Lesson 32 closes the course with a review of all eight chapters together.
